title: Async credit-burn race causing transient quota exceedances
creator: Ruth Chen
description: Summary: We observed short-lived but repeatable transient cases where clients were able to exceed their quota window by a small number of tokens/requests. Root cause appears to be a race in the asynchronous credit-burn path used by the sharded per-key enforcer: duplicate/parallel consume events and delayed cache invalidations allowed short bursts to pass between accounting checkpoints. This affects correctness of usage accounting and rate enforcement (fairness + billing).
steps_to_reproduce: 1) Configure a per-key token bucket with small window (e.g. 60s, 1000 tokens) and enable async credit-burn (default path)
2) From a single API key, fire parallel requests that intentionally straddle the refill boundary (high concurrency at T0, T0+1s)
3) Observe that a subset of requests succeed beyond the expected limit for the window and accounting events show duplicate consumes in the enforcer log

4) Reproduce consistently under a 50-100 rps client with 8 concurrent goroutines in staging; increased likelihood if one or more enforcer shards are experiencing CPU/GC pauses or network latency to Redis/KV cache
observed_evidence: Grafana: rate_limit.burst_exceed_count spiked in us-west-2 during the test run: https://grafana.redwood.example/d/abcd/rate-enforcer?orgId=1
Publish log lines showing duplicate consume_id for same request: https://logs.redwood.example/app/kafka/prod?query=consume_id
Billing delta graph: small positive bias in per-minute token accounting for affected orgs: https://dashboards.redwood.example/d/billing/token-diff
root_cause_analysis: Race between local shard's async emit of a 'consume' message and the central aggregator's reconciliation step. The enforcer shard will optimistically accept a request and emit a consume to the commit log; if the commit log publish is retried or reordered, the central counter may see duplicate increments before dedup is applied
KV cache TTL/refresh can return stale remaining-credit values to the shard which then assumes more tokens are available and performs optimistic accepts
No global monotonic sequencing or idempotency key verification for the credit-burn path, and our de-dupe window is too short relative to observed network jitter
Edge cases amplified when autoscaling moves leases between shards (lease handoff does not drain all in-flight optimistic accepts)
impact_summary: Affects fairness: some customers can issue short bursts above their quota, affecting multi-tenant fairness under load
Affects billing correctness: small over-counts in tokens used can drift billing reports until reconciled
Observed in staging and a small set of high-throughput customers in production (estimated <0.5% of keys active during spike)
No observed data exfiltration or security compromise; strictly accounting/enforcement correctness
short_term_mitigation: 1) Disable async credit-burn for high-throughput keys via feature-flag (ff:disable_async_burn) to force synchronous commit path
2) Increase de-dupe window for consume_id from 2s -> 10s to catch reorder/retry cases
3) Temporarily lower shard acceptance threshold (reject on lower remaining-credit margin) to reduce speculative accepts
4) Communicate to affected customers via support playbook if billing delta > $100 in a day
long_term_fix: 1) Re-architect credit-burn to include monotonic commit sequence numbers per key and use CAS on central counters or a single-writer-per-key lease
2) Add exactly-once semantics via persistent commit-log + idempotent apply (consume_id persisted and checked before apply)
3) Improve lease handoff: drain in-flight optimistic accepts before transferring shard responsibility
4) Add integration tests that simulate network partitions, retries, and reorder to validate no-exceed property under concurrency
5) Add a canary with synthetic high-concurrency client and automated CHAOS tests to detect regressions
acceptance_criteria: No measurable increase in rate_limit.burst_exceed_count in staging under the sustained 100rps multithreaded stress test for 30 minutes
Per-minute token accounting drift between enforcer and billing < 0.01% for the canary orgs during the canary period
Unit and integration tests added to repo covering reorder/retry and lease handoff cases
Change rolled out to production with canary and metrics monitored for 72 hours without regression
implementation_notes: Primary code paths: enforcer/service/async_burn.go, committer/commitlog_writer.go, lease/hand_off.go
Proposed PR will add consume_id persistence in commitlog and a fast index in redis for dedupe checks before apply
Backward compatibility: maintain current behavior behind runtime feature flag and allow gradual migration
Performance trade-off: CAS/strong-commit approach will increase median latency for accepts by ~3-8ms in microbenchmarks — we'll offset with batching improvements in runtime-1.22
timeline_and_updates: 2026-03-08: Issue created by Ruth Chen after stochastic test revealed burst exceedances in staging
2026-03-09: Diego Morales reproduced locally using multithreaded harness; increased de-dupe window reduced occurrences
2026-03-10: Short-term mitigation feature-flag rollout tested in staging (disabled async burn for 3 keys) - reduced burst_exceed_count to 0 during test window
2026-03-11: Draft PR for commitlog idempotency submitted; code review pending from infra team
2026-03-12: Decided on long-term plan: monotonic sequence + idempotent apply; estimate 5 points; canary plan created
rollout_plan: Stage 1: Merge behind FF and run staging canary with synthetic clients for 48h
Stage 2: Enable FF=true for 1% traffic in us-west-2 for 24h, observe metrics
Stage 3: Ramp to 10% and then 50% over 48h if green, then global migration
Rollback: FF off will revert to old behavior; additionally we maintain a per-org emergency reject rule to clamp bursts if billing delta > threshold
tests_to_add: stress: high-concurrency-lease-handoff (verifies no excess accepts during handoff)
notes: Coordination required with billing team — notify before production rollout to reconcile any small historical billing drift
Discuss with runtime team trade-offs for CAS vs single-writer lease (latency vs complexity)
Follow-up: evaluate if similar races exist in embedding/metering path and open separate ticket if found
